transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's about my eating, I suppose. You know, back when I worked at the auto plant—35 years I was there, right on the assembly line—we had exactly thirty minutes for lunch. You ate your ham sandwich, drank your thermos of coffee, and you got right back to it. They don't make cars like they used to, by the way. It's all plastic and computers now. My neighbor's car wouldn't start yesterday because of a software update. Can you imagine? A software update for a car! I told him he should've kept his old Chevy. 

But, uh, where was I? Right, the eating. It's just... what scares me most is that once I start eating, it feels like my hands just keep reaching for more. Even while I’m sitting there telling myself, Tom, stop this right now. It's like I can't stop my own hands. Kind of like how my old dog Buster used to get into the kibble bag if you left the pantry door open, he just couldn't help himself... but I'm a grown man, you know? I should be able to just put the fork down.
When you start eating, do you feel like you can't stop or control how much you eat?

Exactly, doc. Like I was just saying, that's exactly it. I'll be sitting right there at the kitchen table, and my brain is screaming at me, 'Tom, you gotta stop this right now,' but my hands just keep reaching for more. They don't listen to me at all. It’s like they have a mind of their own. 

You know, it really reminds me of muscle memory. Back at the plant, I installed the left-side door hinges for twelve years straight. Twelve years! Even after they finally moved me over to steering columns, I'd wake up in the middle of the night and my hands would be doing the exact motion for the hinges right there in my sleep. My late wife, Martha, she used to laugh and say I was trying to build a Buick in the bedsheets. God rest her soul, she was a wonderful woman. She made the best peach cobbler you ever tasted, too. Actually won a blue ribbon for it at the county fair back in '92. The judges said it was the crust that did it, she used real lard, none of that modern shortening nonsense. 

But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, right, the food. Yeah, it's just like those door hinges. My hands just keep going and going for the food, and I just can't make them quit, no matter how hard I tell myself to stop.
Do you feel upset, ashamed, or guilty after these episodes of eating where you feel like you can't stop?

Oh, doc... guilty doesn't even begin to cover it. The shame is just... it's heavy, you know? It sits right on my chest. Afterward, I just look at the wrappers and the empty plates and I think, Tom, what is wrong with you? 

It's gotten so bad that I've just started hiding away. I used to go down to the community garden every Tuesday morning. We had a nice little group down there. Mostly tomatoes and zucchini, but old Mrs. Higgins, she tried to grow watermelons last year. In this soil! I told her, I said, 'Edna, you're not going to get a watermelon bigger than a softball out of that clay,' and sure enough, she got these little green marbles. We had a good laugh about it. She's moving to Florida next month, actually. Her son bought her a condo down in Boca. 

But, anyway... I haven't been to the garden group in weeks. I've been skipping Sunday dinners with my daughter and the grandkids, too. I just... I can't be around them. I'm either thinking about when I can get back home to eat, or I'm just so disgusted with myself from the night before that I can't look them in the eye. I'm terrified they're going to figure out what I'm doing. A grandfather shouldn't be acting like this. It's just shameful.

latest_inference.note: The patient described feeling a loss of control over eating, eating until uncomfortably full, eating large amounts of food when not hungry, and experiencing shame and guilt afterward. These symptoms align with binge eating disorder (F50.2). The patient does not report symptoms consistent with anorexia nervosa (F50.0, F50.1), such as restrictive eating or fear of gaining weight, and the presentation is specific enough to rule out F50.9.
